messages.subject: Fwd: [stan-dev] hmc_refactor Questions
parts:
Actually, I just figured out a work-around. I can use the base ps_point (which only hold vectors) for storing temporary states (like the initial point in static HMC, or the current sample in NUTS). That way there's only ever one derivation of ps_point (which holds all of the heavy objects) in memory but we don't have to resort to static members or fragmenting the storage.

On Mar 31, 2013, at 4:10 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

>> Are you sure you mean static, and if so, why static?
>> What are the thread safety implications? And what is the
>> alternative? (Static inits are very problematic in C++;
>> at the very least you should understand the basic singleton
>> pattern implementation in C++.)
>
> Yeah, thread safety would be a concern.
>
> Here's the issue: where do you put the (mass) metric? Do you store it in ps_point and duplicate the storage? This is more appropriate for R-HMC where the value of the metric is unique to each point, but then you need m * n^{2} storage, which can quickly become infeasible for large models. Or do you put a single metric in the sampler itself? This makes the sampler stateful (and fragments the state between ps_point and the sampler) and also has the same thread safety issues as you note above. I wasn't thinking about thread safety, and trying to use static to unify the state information without duplicating the actual memory.
>
> Any thoughts?

> Actually, I just figured out a work-around. I can use the base ps_point (which only hold vectors) for storing temporary states (like the initial point in static HMC, or the current sample in NUTS). That way there's only ever one derivation of ps_point (which holds all of the heavy objects) in memory but we don't have to resort to static members or fragmenting the storage.

Great --- that puts the mass metric back conceptually
with the per-sample storage, which seems simpler all around.

The big problem with all of this is that what each sampler
holds in the way of debug information (gradients, mass
matrices, etc.) is very sampler-dependent. So I don't think
there's going to be a great way to generalize from the
outside for a use case that doesn't involve something simple
like serialization. Whatever client is using the sampler
will need to know what its debug information is.

- Bob

Dan and I were talking about this a bit -- can't we get around that by giving the sampler "write_header" and "write_state" methods?  Then gm/command builds a formatter which calls  "write_header" and "write_state" for the model, sampler, etc.  This way we can abstract the specifics of printing each sampler's state into the samplers themselves.
